opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key distinction is between automating programming tasks you've seen before and actually being able to handle novelty. Today's systems are very good at retrieving and recombining patterns from their training data. If you ask for something that resembles a million GitHub repositories, you'll get something that looks plausible. That's useful, but it's not intelligence in the sense I care about.

Genuine AGI in programming would be a system that you could give a problem it has never encountered, in a domain it has never seen, maybe with an API or a language it has to pick up on the fly, and it would figure it out with roughly the same efficiency a skilled human programmer would. Not by having seen a near-identical solution, but by building a model of the problem, forming abstractions, testing hypotheses, and refining them. The hallmark would be skill-acquisition efficiency: how much experience and prior knowledge does it need to become competent at something genuinely new?

Concretely, I'd expect it to be able to take a vague, underspecified goal from a person, ask the right clarifying questions, decompose it into sub-problems, invent new abstractions where existing ones don't fit, and then maintain and evolve that codebase over time as requirements change. That last part matters a lot. Real software engineering isn't writing a function in isolation. It's managing complexity over a long horizon, understanding why a system is structured the way it is, and adapting it without breaking everything.

And I think it would eventually go beyond what we do today. A truly general intelligence wouldn't just write code the way humans write code. It might discover better ways of expressing programs, better abstractions, maybe even better programming paradigms, because it would be doing genuine program synthesis, searching over the space of possible programs guided by deep understanding rather than just pattern-matching on existing human code.

So the test, for me, isn't "can it pass a coding benchmark." Benchmarks can be memorized or gamed. The test is: when you put it in front of something truly novel, does it adapt? If it does, efficiently and reliably, then we're talking about AGI. If it only shines on problems that look like its training data, then what we have is a very impressive, very useful database of programs, but not general intelligence.

r001.rationale: It says AGI should take a vague goal from a person, ask clarifying questions, break it into subproblems, and build the software.

r002.rationale: It expects AGI to maintain and evolve a codebase over time, manage complexity over a long horizon, and adapt code without breaking the system—work it compares with a skilled human programmer’s efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that programming is actually a very good domain to think about this, because it's a domain where current systems already look extremely capable, and yet the gap with genuine intelligence is quite visible if you know where to look.

So what do current models do? They've been trained on essentially all the code ever written and made public. And so when you ask them to write a function, or a class, or even a small application, they're doing something that is closer to retrieval and recombination than to invention. They're pattern-matching your request to the enormous space of programs they've seen, and interpolating. That's very useful. It's a real productivity multiplier. But it's not what I would call intelligence. Intelligence, to me, is the efficiency with which you can acquire new skills and handle situations you have not been prepared for. It's about novelty.

So what would genuine AGI do in programming? A few things.

First, it would be able to pick up a completely new programming language, or a new framework, or a new paradigm, from a small amount of information — the way a strong human engineer does. You give a good engineer a two-page spec of a language they've never seen, maybe a handful of examples, and within a day they're productive in it. They're not relying on having seen a million examples. They're relying on a model of what computation is, what abstraction is, and they map the new thing onto that. Current systems basically can't do this. If the language isn't in the training data, performance collapses.

Second, and this is the more important one, it would be able to solve problems that don't have a known template. Most of the software people write is, frankly, a variation on something that's been written before. That's why LLMs are good at it. But there's a long tail of problems where you actually have to think — where you have to build a model of the problem from scratch, invent a representation, figure out what the right abstraction is, and then implement it. That's the part of programming that is actually hard, and it's the part where current systems are weakest. They're very good at the first ninety percent and very bad at the last ten percent, and the last ten percent is where the intelligence lives.

Third — and I think this is underappreciated — a genuinely intelligent system would be able to maintain and evolve a large codebase over time. Not just write code, but understand the architecture, understand why decisions were made, understand what the invariants are, and make changes that respect them. That requires building and holding a causal model of the system, not just a statistical model of what code tends to look like. Right now, you see models that can generate a plausible-looking patch, but they don't actually know what the system does. They don't have a model of it. They have a model of the surface.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: genuine AGI in programming would mean you could hand the system a problem it has never seen, in a context it has never seen, with limited data, and it would figure it out — the way a strong engineer figures it out. Not by having memorized the solution, but by synthesizing one. And the way you'd measure that is not by how well it does on benchmarks derived from GitHub, because those are contaminated by construction. You'd measure it by giving it tasks that are deliberately novel, where there's nothing to retrieve, and seeing how efficiently it adapts. That's the same philosophy behind ARC, really. The question isn't whether the system can do things it has seen before. The question is how quickly it can do things it hasn't.

r001.rationale: It says genuine AGI would be given a novel problem, figure it out, and implement a solution, which communicates building software from a user-provided description.

r002.rationale: It says AGI should maintain and evolve a large codebase, but does not clearly state that it could handle codebases at the same complexity level as a human software engineer.

astra-6.text:
I would expect it to be able to pick up a programming task in an unfamiliar domain, understand what needs to be done, and figure out how to do it—even if that requires learning new tools or developing an algorithm it hasn’t encountered before.

Writing code is only part of that. Often the difficult part is figuring out what the problem actually is, choosing the right abstraction, and revising your approach when your assumptions turn out to be wrong. You need to be able to test your ideas and recognize when your solution is inadequate.

An AGI wouldn’t have to know every programming language or every codebase in advance. It would have to be able to acquire that knowledge efficiently. That’s the distinction I care about: possessing a collection of programming skills versus being able to develop new skills when faced with a genuinely new problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding and solving unfamiliar programming tasks, but it does not state that AGI would build software from a user's description.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare the complexity of codebases AGI could handle with those handled by a human software engineer.

sol-6.1.text:
I would expect it to be able to pick up a programming task that it has never encountered before, understand what you’re trying to accomplish, and figure out how to do it. And that might involve learning a new language, exploring an unfamiliar codebase, or developing an algorithm that isn’t simply a variation on something it has seen in training.

Programming is interesting because producing code is only part of the problem. You have to formulate the problem, identify the right abstractions, test your assumptions, and adapt when something doesn’t work. A system can be very good at generating familiar patterns of code without being able to do that reliably.

So I would look at how well it handles novelty. Can it acquire the knowledge it needs from a small amount of information and then apply that knowledge to a new situation? That capacity to adapt would be much stronger evidence of general intelligence than performance on a collection of familiar programming problems.

r001.rationale: It says AGI could understand a programming task and figure out how to do it, but does not clearly state that it would build software from a user's description.

r002.rationale: It discusses unfamiliar codebases but does not claim AGI could handle codebases at a human software engineer's level of complexity.
